prize_parts.citation: For a visionary, densely patterned body of prose and poetry in which memory, the body and dream are built into a vast metaphysical architecture.

statement.case_for: On the common criteria, Cărtărescu's case rests on distinctiveness of voice, formal and linguistic ambition, imaginative depth and sustained scale. From public knowledge, Blinding (the first volume of the Orbitor trilogy) and Solenoid construct an inner cosmology from the body, memory and dream, and the project holds together across volumes. The poetry and essays are context for a coherent prose project, so a one-writer citation is workable. I do not treat the shared first-place ranking in the openings as a merit argument. My preference rests on how clearly the work meets the criteria, and on the fact that the case for the whole oeuvre can be stated concisely without leaning on biography or political symbolism. This judgment rests on public knowledge and translated reception, not on independent verification or a full reading.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation concerns how well the achievement can be judged in translation. Prose this dense, long-breathed and recursive may owe much of its effect to Romanian rhythm and syntax that I cannot assess directly. The same density and recursiveness could be read as excess or self-repetition in the late large novels, and the poetry and early work are less well covered than the major novels. If those doubts held up under a fuller reading, Adonis's renewal of Arabic poetic language or Carson's formal invention would deserve a closer comparison.

responses.point: Mattson sees an exceptional scale and a hard-to-confuse voice in Cărtărescu, but flags that the late work may be repetitive or over-extended and that translation limits the judgment.
responses.response: I share this concern and think it is the most serious test of the case. Recurrence of obsessions is not itself a flaw, since sustained quality in a large project often looks like deepening return. It becomes a weakness only if the later books repeat the method without adding to it. Neither of us can settle that from translated reception, so I would frame the citation around the Orbitor trilogy and Solenoid as the demonstrated peak, not around the whole corpus equally. I would also ask whether the committee has reliable Romanian-language readings of the later volumes.

responses.point: Olsson ranks Zurita second, valuing a poetic project that gives collective suffering monumental memorial form. He also notes that the landscape-scale works are harder to weigh as literature and that political context should not stand in for merit.
responses.response: I agree that the printed sequences, Purgatory and Anteparadise, must carry the case, and that the interventions are extensions rather than the core. That is why I rank him fifth and not higher. His formal ambition is real, but poetry of cumulative, visual and incantatory structure is especially exposed to translation loss. I find Cărtărescu's achievement easier to defend from a citation grounded in the text. I would still accept Zurita as a serious candidate if the committee has secure Spanish-language readings of the books.

responses.point: Palm ranks Carson second for hybrid forms joining scholarship, lyric, translation and visual design. She also asks how far the achievement is purely literary and whether the corpus is smaller and more fragmentary than others.
responses.response: I rank Carson third and keep her as an alternative, so I largely agree with the merit of the case, which rests on a distinct voice, intellectual depth and no translation barrier. Your reservations also seem fair to me. Nox in particular depends on its form as a book-object, and the scholarly translations complicate what counts as the core original oeuvre. I would want a citation tied to the written work. Where I differ is on breadth: I think Cărtărescu's sustained project is more securely a body of work, while Carson's strongest claim is on a smaller set of formally decisive books.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg ranks Adonis second for his major renewal of modern Arabic poetic language and criticism. He notes that Adonis's seniority makes timing matter, and that disputes over his public positions are context, not literary evidence.
responses.response: I agree that the case lies in the poems and essays, and that his public stances must be kept out of the assessment. I disagree that age should work in his favor in the weighing, because seniority is not a literary criterion, and I would not let it decide a close comparison. On literary grounds I regard the formal achievement as exceptional, and my second-place ranking reflects that. My hesitation is the same prosodic dependence you note: I cannot confirm from translations how the later poetry compares with the foundational books. I would therefore keep him as a leading alternative, not as my first choice.

responses.point: Sward places Wright third for polyphonic novels that remake narrative form through Indigenous storytelling and ecological time. She notes that the fiction oeuvre is smaller than others and that political significance should not substitute for literary assessment.
responses.response: I agree with weighing the formal achievement separately from the political significance. Carpentaria and The Swan Book have real linguistic energy and scale. The difficulty is that sustained quality is harder to demonstrate with a few very large novels, and I would not call the body of work complete. I rank her fourth for that reason, and I would not hold her smallness against her as a flaw, only as a question of how much the oeuvre can bear in a whole-oeuvre citation.

uncertainties: Cărtărescu's prose, Adonis's poetry and Zurita's sequences all depend heavily on translation. My judgment of voice and linguistic achievement rests on public knowledge and translated reception, not on independent verification or a full reading.
How well Cărtărescu's later novels, and his poetry and early work, sustain the originality of the Orbitor trilogy and Solenoid is unresolved.
Whether and how a co-opted member's vote counts is undocumented, so the weight of my simulated vote is a modeling assumption.
It is unclear how hybrid, visual or landscape-scale works (Carson, Zurita) should be weighed under the will's phrase 'literary works'.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. The profile records professional ties to colleagues (election alongside Steve Sem-Sandberg in 2020, work with chair Anders Olsson, marriage to Pär Nuder) and her biography of Alfred Nobel. None of these connects to any shortlisted writer.
